one_liner: Rust crate of immutable string-to-id dictionaries; front-coded DictIndex comes in smaller than MARISA and XCDAT on the author's 13 corpora.
what_it_does: Builds a static set of strings once, assigns each a dense id in [0, n) (the sorted rank for the ordered indexes), and saves it as a flat blob you can load or memory-map. Seven index types trade size against capability: DictIndex (front-coded, ordered, id to key, prefix and range), HashedDictIndex (DictIndex plus a minimal perfect hash for id), StringIndex (an fst transducer with fuzzy and subsequence search), three perfect-hash maps (Compact, Closed, Perfect) and a character-wise DoubleArrayIndex for matching a lexicon against text. It is not a drop-in for marisa-trie or xcdat: the API is Rust or Python, and from C or C++ there is an opaque-handle C ABI (feature capi, include/lexindex.h) covering build, open/save, id, batched ids, contains and key for six of the seven types.
how_it_is_fast: DictIndex front-codes sorted keys in blocks of 32 to 1024 split into microblocks of 16 to 32, compresses the suffixes with a per-shard FSST-style 255-symbol table or a packed alphabet over a mined phrase dictionary, and recodes mostly non-ASCII keys into an order-preserving 1-2 byte code. A lookup walks the microblock heads and rejects most entries on their one-byte header without decoding them, and the opt-in route_microblocks() trades about 0.5 B/key of memory for 19 to 31 percent faster id. HashedDictIndex adds an in-crate PHast/PTHash-style minimal perfect hash (about 1.92 bits/key) plus a bit-packed rank per slot, so id is a hash and one read instead of a dictionary search.
when_to_use: Static vocabularies, entity catalogs, URL, path or domain lists of 0.5M to 20M keys, where the file and mapped size of the dictionary is the main cost: DictIndex at block 1024 was the smallest structure on all 13 corpora at 1M keys against the harness's MARISA, XCDAT, CoCo-trie, PDT, FST and C2 builds

Hot string-to-id paths on a closed vocabulary that also need id to key, prefix and range: HashedDictIndex answers id in 14 to 61 ns against XCDAT 15's 54 to 449 ns at 1M keys, at a smaller size than XCDAT
Rust or Python services (also Polars through lexindex-polars) that want deterministic, mmap-able blobs and safe loaders for blobs from elsewhere
Prefix counting or range scans: a prefix is an id range in DictIndex, so prefix_count costs two lookups where marisa-trie enumerates every match
when_not_to_use: Exact lookups that must reject unknown keys at trie speed: lexindex's fastest exact structure trails XCDAT 15 on 9 of 13 corpora at 1M keys (5 percent on uuid to 57 percent on pypi), and DictIndex at block 1024, the smallest one, is among the slowest to look up
When the keys change often: every index is immutable, and Overlay edits work only on StringIndex, CompactHashIndex and PerfectHashIndex
Path-like or highly shared keys where MARISA tuned to its smallest (many tries, tiny cache) ties or wins: 0.04 percent apart on paths at 1M, and MARISA is smaller once memory-mapped on 5 of 21 rows
C++ code that needs prefix, range, fuzzy or common-prefix queries: the C ABI exposes only id, ids, contains and key, and leaves out DoubleArrayIndex
Adversarial query streams: the hashes are unseeded and the fingerprint false-positive rate is a design rate, not a HashDoS or security defence (SECURITY.md)

integration.dependencies: fst 0.4 (with levenshtein); optional memmap2 0.9 (mmap feature, default on), optional pyo3 0.29 (python feature); the C ABI builds as a cdylib or staticlib with --features capi
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.85 (edition 2024); Python wheel abi3 for CPython 3.11+
integration.platforms: any Rust target, 32-bit and wasm32-unknown-unknown included (without mmap); benchmarks only on x86-64 (Ryzen 7 5800HS)
integration.thread_safety: Indexes are immutable after build and the README mentions free-threaded CPython use; the C ABI's lexindex_last_error is per thread. No explicit Send/Sync statement was found in what was read.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: it does the same string-to-dense-id job as MARISA or XCDAT but with its own API, ids and blob formats; from C++ it is reachable only through the C handle API

gotchas: HashedDictIndex closed (id_unchecked) and ClosedHashIndex return some valid id for a key that was never inserted. The 14 to 61 ns headline is that mode; use the 8-bit fingerprint (one more byte a key, 2.8 to 7.4x faster than XCDAT 15 per the README) or the dictionary search when strangers can arrive.

Blob formats change across major versions: 2.0 and 4.0 changed the key hash, so pre-4.0 hash blobs and BDX1/BDX2 dictionaries are refused and must be rebuilt from the keys; ids are not stable across key sets. Only 4.5.x is supported, and 4.5.2 fixed a crafted DictIndex blob that could make a routed lookup panic.

Loaders are safe Rust on arbitrary bytes, but StringIndex::from_bytes can panic on a crafted blob that carries a valid checksum (a fuzzer specimen is committed); use from_untrusted_bytes for blobs from strangers. load_mmap is unsafe because the file must not change while it is mapped, and through the C ABI any panic aborts the process.

Keys are raw bytes with no normalization (normalize before build and query); the C ABI rejects non-UTF-8 keys. DoubleArrayIndex refuses corpora that need more than 2^23 slots or keys (7 of 13 at 1M keys).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick lexindex over xcdat when size or id-to-key, prefix and range matter and you can call Rust or a C handle, or when a closed vocabulary makes HashedDictIndex's hashed id usable; keep xcdat (header-only C++) for the fastest exact lookup that rejects strangers on most corpora, and C2 when you need its MARISA, FST or CoCo variants inside a C++ trie framework. For matching a lexicon against Chinese text, DoubleArrayIndex was faster and smaller than darts-clone on the author's jieba measurement, but darts-clone is the drop-in C++ choice.
verified_claims_summary: In the author's own harness (string-index-benchmarks; competitors built at pinned commits with c++ -O3 -march=native -std=c++17, GCC 16.2.1, rustc 1.98.1, lexindex 4.5.2 from crates.io, Ryzen 7 5800HS, 2026-09-26), lexindex's smallest index has the smallest serialized file on 13 of 13 corpora at 1M keys against the campaign's MARISA (1 to 3 tries) and the other tries (words 2.51 vs 2.98 B/key), and HashedDictIndex closed answers member-only probes in 14 to 61 ns against XCDAT 15's 54 to 449 ns. Against MARISA at its smallest, paths is a tie (0.04 percent), and the lexindex README states that MARISA's smallest is 5.8 percent smaller on paths, which conflicts with the harness table.
status_note: Very active single-maintainer project (version 4.5.2, commits through 2026-09-29, 3 stars, no known users, 4 open issues that are all documentation or feature requests); MIT, with a fuzzed loader and a written threat model, but the benchmark author is the library author.
